intro.heading: You know the check was done. Can you show it?
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A registered manager is asked to show the right to work check for a carer who joined a year and a half ago. She knows it was done, because she did it. The scan sits in a shared drive under a file name nobody remembers. The reference number is on a spreadsheet. The expiry date is in a diary that belongs to someone on leave. Twenty minutes later she has found most of it. Nothing was missing in the end. The trouble was that nothing was in one place, and the inspector watched her look.

trail.text: The manager carries out the right to work check at the interview.
She scans the document and saves it in the shared drive.
She notes the reference on the staff spreadsheet.
The folder is renamed and the scan moves with it.
A colleague updates the spreadsheet but not the scan.
Nobody can say which version is the current one.
The date to look at the check again has passed unseen.
"Show me the right to work check for this carer."

trail_close: The check was done properly. What was missing was one place to hold the document and the record together. Here is how a register does that.

faqs.heading: Right to work checks and staff files, answered

groups.group: About the check and the record

items.q: What should we keep as evidence of a right to work check?
items.a: Follow the GOV.UK employer's guide, which explains how to carry out the checks and which documents are acceptable. CareStream stores the document you upload and the details you record.

items.q: Do we need to check again later?
items.a: For some workers a follow up check is needed. The GOV.UK guide explains when. If a time limit applies, set the date on the register and it will warn you 30 days ahead.

items.q: What does Regulation 19 say about staff records?
items.a: Regulation 19 requires that persons employed are of good character, have the skills they need and are fit for the work, and that recruitment procedures are operated effectively. Schedule 3 lists the information that must be available, and it includes proof of identity with a recent photograph.

items.q: What does the View button do?
items.a: It opens the uploaded document in a window over the register, next to the reference number, dates, notes and status, so you can check the file against what is recorded.

items.q: Can staff upload their own right to work document?
items.a: No. The register is admin only, and admins upload the documents.

items.q: Is it a DBS tracker as well?
items.a: Yes. DBS sits on the same register as right to work, registration and references, each with dates, a file and a status.

items.q: Is a scan as good as the original?
items.a: That depends on the check you carried out. The GOV.UK employer's guide sets out what the employer must do and what to keep, so follow it. CareStream holds what you upload.

items.q: Should every document go on the register?
items.a: Hold what your recruitment policy says you rely on. The register has places for DBS, right to work, passport, professional registration and references, and for extras where they apply.

items.q: What if the file we uploaded is the wrong one?
items.a: Upload the right file and check the record against it. The point of the View window is to catch exactly this, by putting the document beside what you recorded.

intro.heading: Every nurse's registration needs a date someone is watching.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: The deputy manager of a nursing home keeps a list of nurses and their revalidation dates in the back of a notebook. When she moves to another service, the notebook goes with her. Three weeks later the new deputy is asked, in passing, how many nurses are due to revalidate in the next quarter. Nobody knows. Everyone is registered, as it turns out. But for a few days nobody could say so with confidence, and that is a worse position to be in than it sounds.

trail.text: A nurse joins and her registration is checked on the register.
Her PIN is written in the staff file.
Her certificate is filed in a folder.
The revalidation date is in the deputy's notebook.
The deputy leaves and the notebook goes with her.
Nobody is watching the date.
The nurse is busy and has not mentioned it.
"Can you show me that your nurses are all registered?"

trail_close: The registration was real. What was missing was a date in a place everyone could see. Here is how the register holds it.

items.q: How do we keep track of nurse revalidation dates?
items.a: Record the revalidation date against each nurse on the workforce register. It shows as valid, expiring within 30 days or expired, and admins get a daily digest email. The NMC explains revalidation on its own site.

items.q: Can we record HCPC and GMC registration too?
items.a: Yes. You choose the body from a list that includes the HCPC, GMC, GPhC and Social Work England, and add Other for anything else.

items.q: What should we keep for each registered member of staff?
items.a: The registration number, a copy of the certificate and the date to check again. Regulation 19 says recruitment procedures must be operated effectively, and the regulation is worth reading in full.

items.q: Does CareStream run an NMC PIN check?
items.a: No. The register records the PIN you enter and the dates. The check itself is yours.

intro.heading: The form exists. The question is whether you can find it, and whether it is right.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: On a quiet Sunday a carer feels unwell and is taken to hospital by ambulance. The senior on duty remembers there is a form for this. It is in a folder in the office, in a drawer that is locked, and the key is with the manager who is away. Eventually someone finds a phone number on an old rota. It turns out to belong to a partner who has since moved. Nobody did anything wrong. The form was completed on day one and never looked at again, and that is how most of them end up.

It goes into her staff file in the office.
The file is put in a locked drawer.

The key holder is on leave.
She is taken ill on a Sunday shift.
Nobody can find a number that works.

faqs.heading: Emergency contacts and staff records, answered

items.q: What should an emergency contact form include?
items.a: At least a name, relationship and a phone number, and a second number where you can. CareStream holds an emergency contact and a next of kin, and lets you mark them as the same person.

items.q: How often should we check emergency contact details?
items.a: There is no set rule, so choose a rhythm you can keep, such as at each supervision. Record the change and the Personal column updates.

items.q: Is next of kin the same as an emergency contact?
items.a: Not always. Someone may want a friend rung first and a relative recorded as next of kin. The register holds both and has a shortcut for when they are the same.

items.q: Who can see staff personal details?
items.a: Admins only.

items.q: Can we see who has not filled in their details?
items.a: Yes. The Personal column shows how many of five sections are complete for each person.

items.q: Does the register store anything about health?
items.a: No. It holds date of birth, emergency contact and next of kin only.

items.q: Should we ask for health information here?
items.a: The register does not hold health information. It holds date of birth, emergency contact and next of kin. Health matters belong in the right place under your own policy.

items.q: Can an emergency contact be someone who is not a relative?
items.a: Yes. It can be anyone the person wants called. Next of kin can be recorded separately, or marked as the same.

items.q: What if a person does not want to give details?
items.a: Record that they declined, in your own notes, and revisit it at supervision. The Personal column will show the gap, which is a prompt to ask again kindly.

items.q: Can we record two emergency contacts?
items.a: The register holds an emergency contact and a next of kin. Use the next of kin entry for a second person where they differ.

items.q: What if someone has no next of kin?
items.a: Record what they tell you and note it. Some people have no family close by, and a friend or neighbour is a perfectly good emergency contact.

items.q: How do I know a number is right?
items.a: Ask the person to read it back when you enter it, and again at supervision. The register can only hold what it is told.

items.q: Is an emergency contact a legal requirement for a staff file?
items.a: Schedule 3 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 lists the information that must be available for each person employed, and an emergency contact is not on that list. Holding one is good practice and a matter for your own policy. Regulation 19 covers recruitment procedures in general.

talk.heading: Questions managers ask about a forgotten PIN

items.q: A carer has forgotten her PIN. What do I do first?
items.a: Open the Staff page, find her name and use the three dots menu. Re-send emails her the same PIN again. It is the quickest option when she can still reach her email.

items.q: When should I regenerate instead?
items.a: When you do not want the old PIN to stay valid, for example if the email might have been seen by someone else. Regenerate makes a new random PIN and emails it. That is how you reset a PIN in CareStream.

items.q: Can I see someone's PIN?
items.a: Only if you choose Show PIN, and that is logged. Administrators never see a PIN in the normal course of things.

items.q: How often can I do this for the same person?
items.a: Re-send, Regenerate and Show are each limited to three an hour per person.

items.q: What if she keeps getting it wrong?
items.a: Five wrong tries locks that person for five minutes. After that she can try again, or you can send her PIN again while she waits.

items.q: Is there a reset PIN button?
items.a: Not by that name. Regenerate is the reset PIN action: it makes a new random PIN and emails it. Re-send keeps the same PIN.

items.q: Do staff choose their own PIN?
items.a: No. CareStream makes a random four digit PIN and emails it. New staff get theirs with their welcome once the account has a tablet.

items.q: Can a locked out carer use the tablet in the meantime?
items.a: No. A connected tablet shows only the Who's using it? screen until someone enters their own PIN, so a locked out carer cannot use Chat or anything else on it until the lock ends or you send her PIN again.

items.q: Does the PIN go to the tablet?
items.a: No. Tablets never receive email or push notifications. The PIN is emailed to the person.

cards.title: It does not remove the need for judgement
cards.body: If you think a PIN has been shared or seen, use Regenerate. The software cannot tell you whether a PIN was misused.

cards.title: It does not decide your policy
cards.body: How long staff may use the tablet, and what your own rule is on sharing a PIN, are your decisions. Write them into your information governance policy.

cards.title: It does not include agency workers
cards.body: Agency workers are not listed on tablets, so they have no PIN to forget.

items.q: What is a forgotten PIN on a shared tablet?
items.a: It is when a member of staff cannot remember the four digit number they use to open their own hub on a tablet. CareStream's Staff page lets an administrator send it again, make a new one or, if needed, show it.

items.q: How do I reset a PIN in CareStream?
items.a: To reset a PIN, use Regenerate in the three dots menu on the Staff page. It makes a new random PIN and emails it to the person. You can also Re-send the same PIN.

items.q: Who sees the PIN?
items.a: The member of staff, in their email. Administrators never see it unless they choose Show PIN, which is logged.

items.q: How long is the lockout?
items.a: Five minutes after five wrong tries.

items.q: Can a stranger lock a colleague out?
items.a: Wrong guesses are limited per person and per poster, so a stranger at a tablet cannot simply lock people out one after another.

items.q: Is the lockout the same on every tablet?
items.a: The lockout is for that person. It is five wrong tries and five minutes.

items.q: What does the email look like?
items.a: It is shown as sent by the administrator, with the PIN in the message. It follows the same setup as other staff emails.

items.q: What if the email address on the record is wrong?
items.a: Correct the email on the Staff page first, then Re-send. A PIN sent to an old address is not safe.

items.q: Do new starters get a PIN?
items.a: Yes, with their welcome, once the account has a tablet.

items.q: Should I tell staff to write their PIN down?
items.a: That is your own policy decision. A written PIN in a pocket is a risk, and Re-send is quick, so most homes are better off encouraging staff to ask rather than write it down.

items.q: Is a four digit PIN secure enough?
items.a: It is one layer. A person also has to connect through the poster, which needs their name and PIN, and wrong guesses are limited. CareStream records and controls access. Your own data protection decisions and the ICO's data security guidance still apply.

items.q: What is an about me profile?
items.a: A plain summary of the person in their own words. In CareStream the resident profile fills the same role, with photos and detail from the family.

items.q: Does it matter which format we use?
items.a: What matters is that it is person centred, up to date and easy to reach. The detail is what helps.

items.q: Who can read the profile on the tablet?
items.a: A member of staff who has entered their own PIN on the connected tablet. Before that, the tablet shows only the Who's using it? screen. This is me is read only.

items.q: Where should the tablet live?
items.a: In a staff area, away from visitors. That is your decision.

items.q: Can the tablet show other things?
items.a: Yes. After a carer enters their own PIN they get their own full hub: Chat, This is me, their training, actions, supervisions and records.

items.q: Why do profiles matter in dementia care?
items.a: The NHS describes how dementia affects memory, communication and behaviour. A profile gives staff the person's own detail to draw on when those change.

items.q: Is there a link to life story work?
items.a: Yes. Life story work is the wider practice of gathering and sharing a person's history. A profile is one product of it.

items.q: How often should we review profiles?
items.a: When something changes, and at a regular point you set, such as with the care plan review.

items.q: What if a family does not want a profile shared?
items.a: Talk to them first and decide what goes in. The profile holds what you choose to record.

items.q: Does CareStream write the profile?
items.a: The profile is yours. The family and key worker supply the detail.

items.q: Can staff use it on a night shift?
items.a: Yes, a connected tablet is open all shift. The home decides where it sits.

items.q: Does it record who read a profile?
items.a: This page does not claim that. What is recorded is set up, connection and PIN events, and every Chat question, against the person and the tablet.

items.a: It is the point at which one team passes information about the residents and the day to the next. It may be spoken, written or both.

faqs.heading: Audit log for a shared tablet, answered

items.q: What is an audit log?
items.a: A record of events, kept so that you can later see who did what and when. In CareStream, tablet set up, connection and PIN events are recorded in it.

items.q: What is an audit trail?
items.a: The same idea in a wider sense: a chain of records that lets you follow an action from start to finish. For a tablet it runs from set up, to connection, to use.

items.q: What is an access log?
items.a: A list of who or what accessed a system. On a shared tablet, the connections, PIN events and chat questions are the access record.

items.q: Are PINs recorded?
items.a: PIN events are recorded: who asked for a PIN to be sent again, regenerated or shown. The PIN itself is not shown to administrators unless an administrator chooses Show PIN, which is logged.

items.q: Is every page the person opens recorded?
items.a: This page makes no such claim. What is recorded is set up, connection and PIN events, and Chat questions.

items.q: Does it record when staff sign out?
items.a: This page does not claim that. A session returns to the Who's using it? screen when staff tap Done or after 5 minutes untouched, with a Still there? prompt at 4 minutes.

items.q: Does the law require an audit log?
items.a: Regulation 17 requires providers to keep records securely and to assess and monitor their service. A log helps you show control. It does not on its own show you meet the regulation.

items.q: What does the ICO say?
items.a: The ICO's guide to data security sets out the idea of appropriate technical and organisational measures. Access control and records of access are part of that.

items.q: Who is responsible?
items.a: The provider. CareStream records and controls access, and your policies and decisions remain yours.

items.q: How often should I look at it?
items.a: A short look each month, and any time a tablet is lost or a member of staff leaves, is a reasonable habit. That is a suggestion, not a rule.

items.q: What if a staff member leaves?
items.a: Remove them from the Staff page as part of your leaver steps, and check that the tablets still show only what you expect.

items.q: Can agency workers be traced?
items.a: Agency workers are not listed on tablets, so they cannot use a tablet and there is nothing to trace.

items.q: What should I tell staff?
items.a: That the tablet records its use, and that every Chat question is recorded against the person and the tablet. Put it in your policy and induction.

faqs.heading: The poster and the QR code, answered

items.q: What is a QR code sign in?
items.a: A way of starting a sign in by scanning a code. In CareStream the code opens a connect page, and a name and personal PIN are still needed, so it is not a sign in on its own.

items.q: Can anyone scan it?
items.a: Anyone can scan it. Scanning gets them to the connect page and no further without a staff member's name and their own PIN.

items.q: Why use a poster at all?
items.a: It makes connecting a tablet quick for staff, without anyone needing to type a long link.

items.q: What is a PIN code for?
items.a: It proves a member of staff is who they say, both to connect a tablet and each time they use it. Each person has their own.

items.q: Where do staff get their PIN?
items.a: It is emailed to them, shown as sent by the administrator. New staff get theirs with their welcome once the account has a tablet.

items.q: What if a PIN is forgotten?
items.a: An administrator can Re-send, Regenerate or Show it from the three dots menu on the Staff page, each limited to three an hour per person.

items.q: Is a poster in a corridor a data protection issue?
items.a: The poster holds no personal data. The risk is access. The ICO's guide to data security sets out the idea of appropriate measures, and limits on guessing and personal PINs are part of that.

items.q: Does the law require a particular sign in?
items.a: No. Regulation 17 asks providers to keep records securely and to monitor their service. How you do that is your decision.

items.q: Who decides where the tablet lives?
items.a: You do. Write it into your policy.

items.q: How many tablets can we have?
items.a: Up to five per account. A tablet is not counted as a staff member or a seat.

items.q: What do we do on day one?
items.a: Add one tablet, print the poster, ask three staff to connect it, and see how it feels. Our guide on night shift policy access shows how a night team can use it.

items.q: Is the connection recorded?
items.a: Yes. Set up, connection and PIN events are recorded in an audit log.

items.q: Can I see whether a tablet is connected?
items.a: The Staff page shows each tablet with a green dot when it is connected and when it was last used.

intro.heading: A ban on phones takes away a route to learning, so give them another.
intro.sub: A scenario we see when a home changes its phone rules.
intro.paragraph: The change was made for good reasons, and the staff understood. But a number of the team had been using their own phones for short lessons and to read their actions. Nobody noticed at first. Then the training matrix showed three people with lessons overdue, and a night carer said she had nothing to use. The manager had a tablet in the office, and nobody had thought to put it in front of the team. The rule was fair, and the gap was an easy one to miss, because the policy changed the way work was done without changing the way learning was done.

talk.heading: Questions managers ask about a phone ban and training

items.q: Do staff really need a phone to do training?
items.a: No. On a shared tablet, each person signs in with their own PIN and opens their own hub with their training. A personal phone is not needed.

items.q: Does the hub on the tablet look different?
items.a: It is the person's own hub. What it shows is their training, actions, supervisions and records.

items.q: What stops one person seeing another's hub?
items.a: Each person needs their own PIN, and the tablet shows nothing without one. The session returns to the Who's using it? screen when they tap Done, or after 5 minutes of being left alone.

items.q: What about a long lesson?
items.a: A session can run for 45 minutes of continuous use at most, and ends after 5 minutes untouched, with a Still there? prompt at 4 minutes. Short lessons suit that. Staff can sign in again to carry on.

items.q: Do we get reminders by phone?
items.a: No. Tablets never receive email or push notifications. Staff emails are sent to the staff member as usual, and you can remind people at handover.

items.q: Can agency workers use it?
items.a: No. Agency workers are not listed on tablets, so they cannot use a tablet at all.

items.q: Does an administrator get admin screens on the tablet?
items.a: No. An administrator who signs in on a tablet gets an ordinary staff session. Admin screens can never be reached from a tablet.

items.a: All paid plans: Starter, Professional and Enterprise. Not the Free plan. Up to five tablets per account.

faqs.heading: Phone bans and training on a shared tablet, answered

items.q: Can a care home ban mobile phones?
items.a: A provider can set its own rules for what staff may do at work, and many homes limit personal phones on the floor. Check your contracts and your own policies, and speak to your HR adviser.

items.q: Why do homes ban phones?
items.a: Common reasons are resident privacy, photographs, distraction and the risk of personal messaging during care. That is a decision for each provider.

items.q: What should a mobile phone use at work policy cover?
items.a: That is for your policy. Many cover where phones are kept, when staff may use them, photography and what happens if the rule is broken. Our social media, phones and photography policy is a starting point.

items.q: What can staff do on the tablet without a PIN?
items.a: Nothing. Before a PIN is entered the tablet shows only the Who's using it? screen, with no Chat and no This is me.

items.q: What needs a PIN?
items.a: Everything else. After their own PIN a person gets their own hub: Chat, This is me, their training and annual training, induction, actions, supervisions, follow ups, CQC questions, progress and records.

items.q: What if mobile phones in the workplace are allowed in some rooms?
items.a: Your policy can say so. The tablet works the same either way. It does not depend on a ban.

items.q: Does the law say anything about staff training?
items.a: Regulation 18 asks providers to make sure staff receive the support, training and development they need to do their work. How you deliver it is up to you.

items.q: Does training on the tablet count?
items.a: It is the person's own hub, so what they complete shows against them. Whether that is enough for your service is for you to judge.

items.q: Where do results show?
items.a: In the training matrix and the person's record, as for any other route.

items.q: What is the quickest way to start?
items.a: Add one tablet, print the poster and ask three staff to connect it. The ICO's data security guidance is worth a read when you decide where it lives.

items.q: What about night staff?
items.a: The tablet is there all shift once connected. Our guide on night shift policy access has ideas for a night team.

items.q: Do we need Wi-Fi?
items.a: This page does not describe network needs. Ask us at a demo.

items.q: How do I stop overdue lessons building up?
items.a: Look at the matrix weekly, remind people at handover, and make a time in the shift. Small regular lessons beat a catch up.
